Introduction



Step 1 : Loading Data

Before all we need to install the packages needed to conduct our analysis should that go in the Intro maybe?

install.packages("readxl")
install.packages("stargazer")
install.packages("ggplot2")
install.packages("performance")

“readxl” extracts the data from excel spreadsheets.
“stargazer” and “ggplot2” are used to create plots.
“performance” package allows to use the model_comparison R function.

We also call their libraries to load the packages.

library(readxl)
library(stargazer)
library(ggplot2)
library(performance)

Next we import the datasets we have chosen to use for our analysis.
We chose these because pur analysis deals with the environment and the relationship between pollution and various economic factors.

The following allow us to measure pollution/CO2 impact :

Renewable_energies_dataset <- read_excel("Renewable_energies_dataset.xls")
C02_emissions_per_capita <- read_excel("C02 emissions per capita.xls")

While these ones are the different economic factors :

GDP_per_capita_dataset <- read_excel("GDP per capita dataset.xls")
Gross_Capital_Formation_percentage_of_GDP_ <- read_excel("Gross Capital Formation (percentage of GDP).xls")
Urban_population_percentage_of_total_ <- read_excel("Urban population (percentage of total).xls")
Total_natural_resources_rents_of_GDP_ <- read_excel("Total natural resources rents (% of GDP).xls")
Trade_of_GDP_ <- read_excel("Trade (% of GDP).xls")
Foreign_direct_investement<- read_excel("Foreign direct investment, net inflows (% of GDP).xls")

Each dataset has data for multiple years. For accuracy we chose to focus on the most recent year (why only 1 year?) with the most amount of data, this proved to be the year of 2021 :

not sure what this does 

recentdata<-data.frame(Country = Renewable_energies_dataset$`Country Name`, 
                       Renewable_energy_consumption = Renewable_energies_dataset$`2021`)
recentdata <- within(recentdata, {
              GDP_per_capita = GDP_per_capita_dataset$`2021`
              Gross_Capital  = Gross_Capital_Formation_percentage_of_GDP_$`2021`
              Urban_pop      = Urban_population_percentage_of_total_$`2021`
              Total_natural  = Total_natural_resources_rents_of_GDP_$`2021`
              Trade_GDP      = Trade_of_GDP_$`2021`
              Foreign_direct_investement= Foreign_direct_investement$`2021`
              C02_emissions  = C02_emissions_per_capita$`2021`
              })
recentdata <-na.omit(recentdata)

Step 2 : Bivariate and Logarithmic OLS


We choose to use the Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) regression because it is considered the Best Linear Unbiased Estimator (BLUE). It has a low variance level, it uses the true values of the estimated alpha and beta and on a large sample it will have a precise estimation.

First, we look at the relationship between Renewable Energy Consumption and GPD per capita.

modA1 <- lm(Renewable_energy_consumption ~ GDP_per_capita, data = recentdata)
stargazer(modA1, type = "text", 
          title ="Table 2: OLS results for Renewable Energy Consumption and GDP per capita")
## 
## Table 2: OLS results for Renewable Energy Consumption and GDP per capita
## ================================================
##                         Dependent variable:     
##                     ----------------------------
##                     Renewable_energy_consumption
## ------------------------------------------------
## GDP_per_capita               -0.0004***         
##                               (0.0001)          
##                                                 
## Constant                     38.460***          
##                               (2.514)           
##                                                 
## ------------------------------------------------
## Observations                    162             
## R2                             0.095            
## Adjusted R2                    0.089            
## Residual Std. Error      25.886 (df = 160)      
## F Statistic           16.744*** (df = 1; 160)   
## ================================================
## Note:                *p<0.1; **p<0.05; ***p<0.01

These results indicate a negative and statistically significant result.

The R-squared value is of 0.095 which indicates that GDP per capita explains approximately 9.5% of the variation in renewable energy consumption across the 162 countries included in our sample.

The coefficient is -0.0004 ; which assumes a negative correlation ; we can infer that countries with higher GDP per capita tend to have lower shares of renewable energy consumption, on average.

Though significant, the p-value is below the conventional 0.05, this result indicates that there are other variables that probably play a bigger role on the consumption of renewable energy.

probably more and better analysis to be done


It is also important to plot the relationship to assess the fit of the model used.

plot(recentdata$GDP_per_capita, recentdata$Renewable_energy_consumption,
     xlab = "GDP per Capita", 
     ylab = "Renewable Energy Consumption",
     main = "Relation between GDP per Capita and Renewable Consumption",
     col="blue")
abline(modA1, col="red", lwd=2)

The plot shows the Gauss-Markov assumptions to be somewhat respected.

Thought increase the precision and readability of the model we add the log function to the GDP.

modA2 <- lm(Renewable_energy_consumption ~ log(GDP_per_capita), data =recentdata)
stargazer(modA2, type = "text", 
          title ="Table 3: OLS results for log(Renewable Energy Consumption) and log(GDP per capita)")

Step 3 : Multivariable models and model selection

Finally, we are going to do a multivariate OLS explain why

mod_multiple <-lm(Renewable_energy_consumption ~ 
               log(GDP_per_capita) +
               Urban_pop + 
               Gross_Capital + 
               log(Trade_GDP) + 
               Total_natural +
               Foreign_direct_investement , 
               data = recentdata)
stargazer(mod_multiple, type = "text", 
          title ="Table 11: Multivariable OLS results for Renewable Energy Consumption and the other variables")
##

Really good performing model, and log(GDP_per_capita) remains highly significant,but Trade_GDP and Urban_pop lose significance. We are going to compare the models we have with the R function

model_comparison <- compare_performance(modA1, modA2, modA3, modA4, modA5, modA6,
                                        modA7, modA8, modA9, mod_multiple, rank = TRUE)
print_md(model_comparison)
